I've been using these tools for a few months on a mid-sized Python codebase, and the pattern is consistent: they're excellent at the first 80% and quietly dangerous for the last 20%. Boilerplate, test scaffolding, regex, and translating a function from one language to another are all things it does well. The problem is that its output looks finished even when it isn't. It will confidently call an API method that doesn't exist, or write a loop that passes the happy-path test and fails on empty input, and nothing in the code signals that. You have to read everything with the same skepticism you'd give a fast junior's first PR, which, honestly, is more work than it sounds when the diff is large.

I think the more interesting question is what happens to the skill ladder. Writing the boring code was how a lot of us learned to read code, notice edge cases, and build intuition about what breaks. If the tool takes over that part, people can ship working software without ever developing the judgment needed to tell when it's wrong. That doesn't make the tool useless, but it argues for treating it like a power tool that needs a reviewer who already knows the material, and for teams being deliberate about how juniors use it.

Most startups underprice because they anchor on cost and on what they imagine customers will tolerate, rather than on the value the product delivers. Founders often pick a price that feels "fair" or "competitive" without testing it, and they worry that a higher number will kill conversions. But the people who buy early are rarely the price-sensitive crowd. They're usually the ones with a painful problem and a budget, and a low price can signal that the product is a toy, an afterthought, or likely to disappear. Low prices also attract the customers who churn first and complain most, which makes the business harder to run.

There's also a asymmetry that founders underestimate. Raising a price later is hard, because existing customers feel betrayed, but lowering one is easy. Starting high and discounting for specific cases gives you room to learn. Starting low locks you into a number that's expensive to escape. Many companies that later "discovered" their pricing power had simply never tested a higher tier. A useful exercise is to ask what a customer would pay to avoid the problem for a year, then price well below that to leave them a clear win.

Finally, underpricing distorts the rest of the business. Low revenue per customer forces you into high-volume sales, thin margins, and heavy support loads, which leaves little money for the work that actually improves the product. It also changes who you hire and what you optimize for. Charging more doesn't just increase revenue; it tends to make the company more serious about serving the customers who pay, and it gives you the resources to become the product those customers were willing to buy.

Most founders price low because they're scared of the wrong number. They picture a prospect asking "why so expensive?" and they hear that question in their head for weeks. What they don't picture is the prospect who bounces because the price made them wonder if the thing was a toy. Price is one of the few signals buyers use to judge quality before they've used anything, and a low number quietly tells them "this is probably not serious" or "this will disappear in a year."

The other problem is that low prices attract the customers who cost the most. They ask for the most hand-holding, they churn when something goes wrong, and they argue about every invoice. A $19/month plan sounds like a way to get volume, but supporting 400 of those people can eat the time you needed for the 20 who would have paid $300 and actually stuck around. I've seen a couple of companies raise prices by 3x and lose almost nobody, mostly because the people who left were the ones who were never going to become real customers anyway.

My advice is to pick a number that makes you slightly nervous and then talk to five customers about it before you change anything. If nobody flinches, you were leaving money on the table. If a few do flinch, ask them what they'd need to see to pay it. Those answers are usually more useful than any pricing page benchmark, and they tell you what to build next.

Honestly, I think "AI replaces junior devs" is the wrong frame. What's changing is the shape of the first two years. A junior used to spend a lot of time on tasks that were tedious but educational: writing CRUD endpoints, chasing down a null pointer in someone else's code, slowly learning what a codebase actually does. Models now handle a lot of that grunt work faster than any junior can. That's real pressure on the entry-level job postings, and I'd be lying if I said otherwise. But the work that made juniors valuable was never just the output. It was the ramp-up, and the ramp-up still has to happen somehow.

The thing I worry about is the pipeline. If companies stop hiring juniors because a senior with Copilot can do the work, then in five years there are no mid-level engineers, and in ten there are no seniors. Some teams are already noticing this. The people who become great debugging distributed systems at 2am are the ones who spent years doing small, unglamorous fixes and building intuition from failure. You can't shortcut that by prompting well. Someone has to pay for the learning, and right now it's unclear who.

My guess is the junior role survives but changes character. The valuable juniors in five years will probably be the ones who use these tools to go deep rather than to skip steps: asking why the generated code works, reading the stack traces instead of pasting them back, and reviewing output critically. The ones who treat the model as a black box will struggle, and so will the companies that hire them without any plan for how they'll grow.

Our numbers made this decision easier than I expected. We were spending a little under a third of our infrastructure budget on egress and managed-database markups, and most of our traffic was steady-state, so the elasticity we paid for was going unused. The migration was not free. We had to rebuild our observability stack, our CI runners, and the backup pipeline, and we lost about two months of feature velocity. But the hardware payback period came out to roughly fourteen months, and the cloud bill had been climbing every quarter without a corresponding increase in load.

What people underestimate is the operational cost of leaving. Cloud providers sell you the managed service and the expertise to run it, and when you bring things back in-house, you inherit both the pager and the knowledge gap. We kept a small platform team on the cloud for the first six months as a safety net, and I'd recommend that to anyone. The other thing I'd flag is that a lot of "cloud vs. on-prem" debates skip the middle option of colo with leased bare metal, which gave us most of the cost savings without buying and racking our own servers.

That said, I wouldn't generalize from our case. If your traffic is bursty, your team is small, or your compliance story depends on managed services, the math could look very different. The honest answer is that the cloud is expensive in a predictable way and self-hosting is expensive in an unpredictable way, and the right choice depends on which kind of unpredictability your organization can absorb.

We did something similar two years ago, moving our main Postgres and a bunch of batch jobs off RDS and onto three beefy bare-metal boxes in a colo. The hardware cost was about what we used to pay AWS in a single month, so the payback was fast. The part people underestimate is the boring stuff. We had to relearn backups, replication failover, and disk monitoring, and for the first few months every little alert felt like a fire. It's calmer now, but it's real ongoing work that used to be somebody else's problem.

I don't think the lesson is "cloud bad." Our bursty workloads, like the CI runners and the image processing that spikes on Mondays, still live in the cloud, because paying per minute beats owning idle capacity. The savings came from moving the steady, predictable stuff that we'd been paying a markup on for years. If your baseline load is flat and you have someone who likes this kind of work, the math is hard to ignore. If you don't have that person, the bill you save can disappear fast into on-call hours.

The "AI beats radiologists" headlines age badly once you look at how the studies were built. Most of the impressive numbers come from retrospective datasets, often curated from a single hospital, with labels pulled from the same reports the model was trained on. Performance drops when the model meets scanners from another vendor, different patient demographics, or a different protocol, and external validation is still the exception. A lot of "superhuman" results are also AUC comparisons against a reader who never saw the clinical history, which isn't how radiologists actually work.

The bigger problem is that a high-accuracy classifier doesn't tell you what happens to patients. Few of these papers measure whether the tool changed diagnoses, reduced time to treatment, or improved outcomes, and some FDA-cleared products have been approved on the basis of sensitivity and specificity alone. Deployment also brings alert fatigue, automation bias, and liability questions that a benchmark never captures. I'd like to see more prospective, multi-site trials with outcome endpoints before treating these systems as more than triage aids.

None of this means the field is useless. Narrow tools like diabetic retinopathy screening and some fracture detection have shown real workflow value in controlled settings. The problem is the gap between that and the framing of "radiologists will be replaced," which the evidence doesn't support yet.

Most of the "AI beats radiologists" papers I've read compare a model against a single radiologist reading retrospective images with the labels already known, which is a very different task from a busy reader triaging a live queue. The chest X-ray and mammography studies that got the big headlines often had the labels leak in through the dataset construction, or they used a reference standard that was itself just the original clinical report. I worked on a project a few years ago where we got a model to 0.95 AUC on an internal set, then watched it fall to about 0.78 when we ran it on images from a different scanner vendor at a different hospital. Nobody was lying. The model had learned the scanner's compression artifacts and the institution's labeling habits along with the pathology.

What bugs me most is that the FDA-cleared products are mostly narrow triage tools that flag a study for priority reading, and they're useful for that. The marketing around them drifts toward "diagnosis," and then the press release turns into a claim that AI will replace a specialty. Radiology residency applications are still going up, which is a funny thing to watch if you believed the 2016 Hinton prediction that we'd stop training radiologists. The hard part was never pattern matching on the pixels. It's knowing the patient, knowing the prior studies, and knowing what the referring clinician is actually worried about.

I don't want to be the guy who says it's all useless, because some of these tools do measurable good in stroke pathways and diabetic retinopathy screening, where the task is narrow and the prevalence is high enough that a sensitivity-focused filter pays off. My complaint is about the gap between what gets validated prospectively and what gets sold on the strength of a retrospective AUC.

Enterprise software is bad mostly because the people who pick it are not the people who use it. A VP signs off after a vendor demo built on a clean sample dataset and a slide deck, and the purchasing criteria become checkboxes: SSO, audit logs, "AI-powered," compliance certifications. Nobody on the buying committee has to spend eight hours a day clicking through the thing, so the metric that matters, how fast a real person can do their job, never enters the decision. The vendor's incentives point the same way. Their customer is the buyer, and lock-in, per-seat pricing, and proprietary data formats are features from the seller's side, so the product is optimized to be hard to leave rather than pleasant to use.

The second problem is that every feature request is a negotiation with a different stakeholder. Finance wants a field, legal wants a approval step, the regional team wants a custom report, and the product team wants to ship something for the next conference. Each addition is individually reasonable and collectively ruinous, because nobody owns the whole experience. Configuration becomes the escape valve: instead of making good decisions, the software exposes a thousand settings so that the decisions can be deferred to the customer's admin, who then spends years in a forms-within-forms maze. Over time the product accumulates the scar tissue of every sales cycle, and the codebase gets slower, the UI gets more crowded, and the original designers are long gone.

Finally, the feedback loop is broken. Consumer software dies quickly when people stop using it, so it has to earn its keep every day. Enterprise software survives on contracts that run for three to five years, and the cost of a bad tool is spread across thousands of employees who have no way to vote with their wallets. Their complaints go to an internal help desk that files tickets against the IT department, not the vendor, and the vendor rarely hears about it until a renewal is at risk. The result is software that is technically capable of almost anything and practically pleasant at almost nothing, and everyone involved, from the buyer to the vendor's account team, can tell themselves it's working.

I think most of it comes down to who the software is actually built for. The person who picks it is almost never the person who uses it every day. A VP signs off after a three-hour demo and a spreadsheet of checkboxes, so the product gets optimized for the RFP matrix: "supports SAML," "has an audit log," "can be configured to do X." Nobody gets scored on whether the checkout flow makes sense to a tired claims adjuster at 4pm. So you end up with forty settings menus, each one a little admission that somebody decided not to make a decision, and the whole thing feels like it was designed by committee because it was.

The other piece is that the incentives are upside down all the way down. The vendor's sales team closes deals by promising customization, so the product team builds escape hatches instead of opinions. Each big customer gets a custom field or a special report, and those pile up into a codebase nobody fully understands. Meanwhile the integration story is "we have an API" which means every workflow touches three systems that were each bought separately and never talked to each other, and someone at the company is paid to paste CSVs between them. Support contracts and renewal pricing reward lock-in, not usability, so there's no pressure to make the thing pleasant to leave or even to use.

I'd also blame the switching cost itself. Once a company has trained 2,000 people and migrated ten years of data, the software can get worse for a long time and still not die. Users complain, the complaints go into a backlog, and the backlog is ranked by the customers paying the most, who are the ones who asked for the weird stuff in the first place. It's not that anyone is trying to make bad software. It's that every individual decision is reasonable given its local incentives, and the sum of those decisions is something nobody would have chosen if you asked them up front.

Subscription fatigue on mobile is real, but I think the deeper problem is that apps quietly changed what they're selling. A few years ago you paid once for a flashlight app or a note-taker and it did one thing. Now the same category charges $4.99 a week for "premium" features that are mostly a paywall around things that used to be free, and the cancel button is buried three menus deep or routed through the App Store settings where most people never look. The economics make sense for the developer: recurring revenue is predictable and investors like it. But the result is that I have a dozen small charges I forgot about, and each one is too small to justify the effort of hunting it down.

What bothers me most is the asymmetry. Signing up takes one tap, often with a free trial that auto-converts, while canceling requires finding the right screen, sometimes calling support, and occasionally getting a "are you sure?" dark-pattern screen with a discount offer. Regulators in some places have started forcing "click to cancel" rules, which tells you how common the problem got. I'd like to see a simple norm where any subscription can be canceled as easily as it was started, and where apps have to send a reminder before a trial converts.

I also think many of these apps would be better as one-time purchases or clearly tiered annual plans for users who want them. Subscriptions make sense for services with real ongoing costs, like cloud sync, server-side processing, or content that keeps updating. They make much less sense for a calculator, a photo filter, or a habit tracker that stores everything on the device. Until more developers draw that line honestly, I'll keep auditing my App Store subscriptions once a quarter and feeling mildly annoyed every time I do.

I think the real problem isn't that the data got stolen, it's that it was kept at all. Most of the stuff in these breach notices, like SSNs, dates of birth, and security questions, was collected for a one-time check and then just sat in a database for years. If they'd deleted it after verification, there'd be nothing to leak. Every time one of these happens, I wonder how many people at the company knew that old records were still around and decided it wasn't worth the effort to purge them.

The "we take your privacy seriously" boilerplate in the notice is also useless. What I'd actually want to see is how long the attacker was inside before anyone noticed, whether the access came through a vendor or an employee account, and whether they're still using MFA on internal admin tools. Credit monitoring for two years is a nice gesture, but it mostly covers the company's legal exposure, not the actual harm to me.

Hi, I hit this same problem on my end. When I generate images at 768 pixels on a single dimension, the Stable Diffusion web UI runs out of memory and the generation fails partway through. Smaller sizes like 512 work without trouble on the same setup, so the jump to 768 seems to be the point where VRAM is exhausted. I have not yet tried the low VRAM or medium VRAM startup flags, so I don't know whether they would help, but I wanted to add this data point in case it helps narrow down the threshold for others reporting similar failures.

Changing the default learning rate from 1e-3 to 3e-4 should make early training noticeably more stable, especially for the larger configurations where the loss spiked in the first few hundred steps. I reran the small and medium baselines with the new default, and both converged to within 0.2% of the previous validation loss while showing smoother loss curves. The one tradeoff is that the smallest model now takes roughly 15% more steps to reach the same loss, so users running short schedules may want to bump the warmup or set the rate explicitly.

I'd suggest we also add a note to the changelog and the config docs so the new default isn't a silent change for anyone pinning their runs to the old value. Happy to make those edits in this PR if you'd like, or split them into a follow-up.

Apps that are free to download usually make money in a few main ways:

**1. Ads.** Companies pay to show you ads inside the app. Some apps show banners, others show short videos between levels, and advertisers pay per view or per click.

**2. In-app purchases.** You can pay for extras like power-ups, skins, or removing ads. Many games rely on this, and a small share of players often spends most of the revenue.

**3. Subscriptions.** Apps like streaming services or fitness trackers charge a monthly or yearly fee for premium features.

**4. Selling your data.** Some apps collect information about how you use them and share it with advertisers or data brokers. Reputable companies disclose this in their privacy policies.

**5. Upselling.** The free version works as a trial that pushes you toward a paid plan.

**6. Partnerships.** Apps may earn commissions from affiliate links, such as shopping or travel apps that get a cut of each sale.

So "free" usually means you pay with your attention, your data, or money spent later on extras.

Start by calculating your costs. Add up what you need to earn per year, including taxes, software, insurance, and the hours you'll spend on admin and marketing, then divide by the billable hours you realistically expect to work. That gives you a floor rate.

Next, research what others charge. Look at freelancer profiles on Upwork or similar sites, and ask a few developers in your area what they charge. As a beginner, you can reasonably price below experienced freelancers, but not so low that you can't sustain the work.

For a first project, consider a fixed price instead of hourly. Estimate the hours carefully, add a 20–30% buffer for surprises, and multiply by your rate. Clearly define the scope in writing, including the number of revisions, so you don't end up working for free.

Ask for a deposit, typically 30–50% upfront, before you start. This protects you from clients who disappear.

Finally, treat the first project as a learning experience. Track your actual hours so you can price the next one more accurately.

Everyone who predicted fully autonomous cars by 2018, or then by 2020, was working from the same flawed assumption: that the hard part was the last 10% of driving, and that enough sensors and training data would close the gap. The gap turned out to be the long tail of weird, rare situations that human drivers handle through common sense, eye contact, and social negotiation. A plastic bag blowing across the road, a cop waving traffic through a red light, a construction worker with a hand signal the training set never saw. Each of those is trivially solved by a person and stubbornly hard for a system that has only seen patterns. Demos on curated routes in sunny cities looked like proof of concept, but scaling to rain, snow, unmapped rural roads, and edge cases took far longer than the press releases suggested.

The timelines also ignored how much of the problem lives outside the software. Regulators, insurers, and liability lawyers have to decide who is responsible when something goes wrong, and those answers move at the speed of legislatures, not GitHub commits. Hardware costs, sensor redundancy, and the need for remote human operators to unstick vehicles have all added friction. Meanwhile, the companies that did reach real driverless operation did so by narrowing the problem: geofenced service areas, heavy HD mapping, and conservative operating domains. That is useful, but it is a long way from the "sleep in your car on the commute" vision that got hyped.

I don't think the technology is a dead end, and the progress over the last decade is real. But the honest lesson is that driving is a deeply open-ended problem, and we underestimated how open-ended it was. The people who were most confidently wrong were often the ones closest to the demos, not the ones who had spent time on the hard cases. Expect incremental, city-by-city deployment for a while longer, and be skeptical of any date that doesn't come with a clear account of what happens in the snow.

Honestly the "two years away" line has been running since about 2015, so at this point I just mentally add a decade to any timeline. What gets me is how the goalposts moved without anyone admitting it. Early on the promise was that cars would drive themselves everywhere, in all weather, with nobody paying attention. Now we have geofenced robotaxis in a handful of cities that still need remote operators to unstick them when they freeze up at a weird intersection or a construction cone. Those are real achievements, and I've ridden in one that was genuinely impressive, but it's a different product than what was sold to investors and to my uncle who bought a Tesla in 2016 for "full self-driving."

I think the core problem is that the last 5% of the driving task is nearly all of the difficulty. Highway lane-keeping and stop-and-go traffic were solved well before most people expected. The long tail is what kills you: a kid chasing a ball, a cyclist doing something nobody trained for, a flooded underpass, a police officer waving traffic through with hand signals. Demos are built on curated routes, and the gap between a good demo and something that can handle every bad day across a whole country is enormous. Nobody on a stage can show you that gap.

That said, I don't think the answer is that it'll never happen. Waymo is doing real paid rides in several metros with a track record that's actually measurable, and that's more than I expected to see by now. My guess is we get there in pieces, with robotaxis in dense cities with good mapping first and personal cars that can drive anywhere much later, if ever. The people who promised otherwise weren't lying exactly, they just assumed the hard part was the easy part.

Honestly, the "remote work is dead" and "remote work is the future" takes both miss what actually changed. Remote work didn't create a new kind of company so much as expose which companies already had good written communication and clear ownership. The teams that thrived in 2020 were usually the ones that had already moved decisions into docs and issue trackers. The teams that struggled were running on hallway conversations and "quick calls" that nobody recorded, and removing the hallway just revealed how much of their coordination was invisible.

I think the real split now is less about office versus home and more about whether a company treats asynchronous work as a discipline or as an afterthought. Pure remote shops often end up with better documentation than their office-based peers, simply because they had no choice. Hybrid setups, on the other hand, can quietly recreate the old problem: the people in the office make decisions in the room, and the remote folks get a summary a day later and feel like second-class employees. If you're going to have a hybrid policy, the only version I've seen work is one where you assume everyone is remote and let the office be an optional bonus.

As for the people who want to go back, I'd be cautious about dismissing them entirely, but also about taking their reasons at face value. Some of the desire for the office is about mentorship, junior people learning by absorbing how senior folks think, and that's a legitimate loss that remote teams have to deliberately replace. Some of it is about managers who never learned to manage outputs rather than presence. Separating those two motives would make the debate a lot more productive than arguing about badge swipes.
